title: Roots and patterns (Semitic morphology)
body: Most Arabic and Hebrew words are built from a **root** of (usually) three consonants that carries a core meaning, poured into a **pattern** of vowels and extra letters that carries a grammatical meaning.
k-t-b = writing: Arabic كَتَب katab 'he wrote', كِتاب ktāb 'book', مَكتَب maktab 'office/desk', كاتِب kātib 'writer'. Hebrew uses the same root: כָּתַב katav 'he wrote', מִכְתָּב mikhtav 'letter'.
Learning to see roots turns one new word into a family of half-known words. Learn patterns as templates: maCCaC = place of (maktab, madras-), CāCiC = doer (kātib).

langs.ar: Explicit from Unit 5; every word shows its root when it has a clear one.
langs.he: Hebrew binyanim and mishkalim are the same idea; Arabic roots are linked.

title: Sentences without 'to be' (zero copula)
body: Many languages don't say 'is/are' in the present: 'I student', 'the house big'.
Arabic, Hebrew, Russian, and (often) Sanskrit and Ancient Greek do this. The verb appears in the past and future.

langs.ar: أنا طالب ʔana ṭālib = I (am a) student.
langs.grc: Greek often omits ἐστί in short statements.

title: Grammatical gender
body: Nouns belong to classes (masculine/feminine, sometimes neuter) that adjectives, verbs and pronouns agree with.
Spanish already does this: el libro nuevo / la casa nueva.

langs.ar: Feminine usually ends in ـة (-a/-e). Verbs and adjectives agree.
langs.he: Feminine often ends in ה- or ת-.
langs.la: Three genders; like Spanish plus neuter.
langs.ta: Tamil gender is semantic (rational beings) rather than formal.

title: Definite articles
body: 'The' marks something both speakers can identify. Some languages attach it to the word, some have none.

langs.ar: ال al-/il- is prefixed and assimilates to 'sun letters' (الشمس ish-shams).
langs.la: Latin has no article: context does the work.
langs.grc: ὁ ἡ τό, inflected for case.

title: Possession by juxtaposition (construct state / iḍāfa)
body: 'House-of the-teacher': the possessed noun comes first and loses its own article; only the final noun can be definite.

langs.ar: بيت المعلّم bēt il-mʕallem 'the teacher's house'. ة is pronounced -it in construct.
langs.he: סמיכות smikhut: בית המורה beit ha-more.

title: Tense vs aspect
body: Some verb systems mark *when* (tense); others mark whether an action is completed or ongoing (aspect). Arabic perfect/imperfect is mostly aspect; Levantine adds b- for habitual/present and ʕam for progressive.

langs.ar: katab (completed) vs byiktob (habitual) vs ʕam yiktob (in progress).
langs.grc: Greek aorist vs present stem is aspect.
langs.zh: Mandarin 了 / 过 / 在 mark aspect, not tense.

title: The dative case (indirect object: 'to/for someone')
body: The dative marks the recipient or beneficiary: 'I gave the book **to Maria**'.
Spanish shows it with le / a: le di el libro a María.

langs.ar: Arabic uses the preposition لـ la-/li-: إلي ʔilī 'to me'.
langs.he: Preposition ל le-: לי li 'to me'.

title: Bare verb after 'want / must / can'
body: After verbs like want/must/can, many languages use a special or reduced verb form (Spanish: quiero que vengas).

langs.ar: Levantine drops b-: bḥibb 'I like' but biddi ḥibb… / lāzim rūḥ 'I must go'.
